title.narrative: Promoting inclusion, right to education and Early Childhood and Care Education in West Africa

description.narrative:
In West and Central Africa, nearly 39 million children do not attend school, with the region accounting for one-third of the world's out-of-school children of primary age, and one-fifth of those of secondary age. There are marked disparities in access to quality education, particularly between urban and rural areas as well as between rich and poor households. Schools in rural and disadvantaged areas suffer from poor conditions or non-existence of proper school buildings and facilities, including toilets, desks and chairs. In West Africa, only seven out of 15 countries have ratified the UNESCO Convention against Discrimination against Education (1960), while 4 of them have accepted it.. At lower secondary level, gender disparities are widening overall, especially in countries that have not yet achieved parity at the primary level. Furthermore, as the population of young people aged 0-25 is set to increase from 63 million in 2022 to 119 million in 2025 in the region, education systems will be confronted with heavy demographic pressure, making it difficult to ensure inclusion and the right to education for all. Early childhood care and education (ECCE) lays the foundation for subsequent learning and wellbeing, promoting readiness for primary school; however, access to pre-primary education remains insufficient and unequal, with only 22% of children are enrolled in West Africa. More systemic efforts and collaborations are needed to accelerate progress in ECCE so that children are empowered to begin and continue their learning and development trajectories on a solid basis nurtured by quality care, education and protection.
To this effect, UNESCO supports countries in enshrining the right to education and incorporating it into their policies and practices in accordance with existing international and regional frameworks and commitments. It assists countries in promoting inclusion in education, with particular attention the most vulnerable and marginalized groups. Key activities include the integration of specific guidelines for learners with disabilities and vulnerable groups into current state-level education plans and teaching-onboarding processes. Moreover, UNESCO supports the expansion of access to quality ECCE, in line with relevant international and regional frameworks and commitments such as the Tashkent Declaration and the Commitments to Action for the Transformation of ECCE adopted at the 2022 World Conference on ECCE by Member States. The Declaration calls for the implementation of commitments such as at least one year of free, compulsory, high-quality pre-primary education, and the target of allocating at least 10% of education expenditure to pre-primary education. UNESCO supports evidence-based assessment, policy dialogue and prioritization in ECCE in selected countries.
